title: Purushottama Dasa (Nagara Purushottama)
html:
The Son of Sadashiva Kaviraja

Among those whom the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” calls branches of Nityananda's tree are a father and son of the Vaidya community — Sadashiva Kaviraja and Purushottama Dasa. Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of them in a single verse:

“Sri Sadashiva Kaviraja was a great soul, and Sri Purushottama dasa was his son.” (CC, Adi 11.38)

Vrindavana Dasa, too, names them side by side as he lists Nityananda's companions:

“Sadashiva Kaviraja was supremely fortunate. His son was named Purushottama Dasa.” (CB, Antya 5.741)

Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” calls him Nagara Purushottama; the biographies call him Sri Purushottama Dasa, Sri Purushottama Thakura, Purushottama Dasa Thakura and Purushottama-Nagara. Manohara Dasa in the “Anuraga-valli” calls him “Sri Purushottama Mahashaya, dear to Nityananda”; the Sanskrit vandana ascribed to Srila Jiva Gosvami calls him “the Dasa named Purushottama,” and his disciple Devakinandana calls him “my chosen master” and “my guru.”1

His father, Sadashiva Kaviraja, is Chandravali in Krishna's pastimes:

“Chandravali, who once in Vraja was Krishna's supreme beloved, is now in the land of Gauda Kaviraja Sadashiva.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 156)

The “First Vandana,” ascribed to Vrindavana Dasa, says the same: she whom the Puranas extol as Chandravali, all know as Sadashiva Kaviraja (pt. 4, vv. 47–48). Father and son belonged to the Vaidya community, the physicians, and the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” calls Sadashiva supremely fortunate.

Purushottama's grandfather was Kamsari Sena, whom Krishnadasa Kaviraja likewise names among the branches of Nityananda (CC, Adi 11.51). In the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” Kamsari Sena stands fifth in a list of associates and Ratnavali fifth in a list of gopis (194, 200), and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” says plainly that Kamsari Sena is Ratnavali of Vraja. There he also writes that this ancestor was called Sambarari as well. Kamsari Sena is said to have lived in Guptipara, though nothing of him is to be found there now.

Thus in one family four generations in a row — Kamsari Sena; Sadashiva Kaviraja, his son; Purushottama Thakura, born to Sadashiva; and Kanu Thakura, born to Purushottama — were perfected associates and devotees of Gaura. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, and the biographies after him, remark how rarely such a thing is found: it is a special mercy of the Lord upon the family.

Dama, Krishna's Friend

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes Karnapura tells us:

“The son of Sadashiva named Nagara Purushottama, born in a family of Vaidyas, is Dama, a cowherd of Vraja.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 131)

Dama is one of Krishna's cowherd friends, and in Vraja Purushottama is a companion of His childhood games.2 That is why he is counted among the twelve gopalas — the cowherd boys of Vraja who came into Gaura's pastimes as Nityananda's companions. Lochana Dasa in the “Chaitanya-mangala” lists them thus:

“Ramadasa, Gauridasa and Sundara, Krishnadasa, Purushottama, Sri Kamalakara, Kala Krishnadasa and Uddharana Datta — the twelve cowherd boys (gopalas) of Vraja: such is their greatness.” (“Chaitanya-mangala,” Sutra-khanda 8.626–627)

In the lists of the twelve gopalas given in the biographies he stands next to his namesake, Purushottama Pandita of Navadvipa: in one he is eighth and the Pandita ninth, in another the Pandita is eighth and Purushottama tenth. In the list of the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” the eighth line reads “Purushottama Dasa, Nagara Purushottama — Dama,” and the ninth “Purushottama Dasa — Stokakrishna”: these are two different persons.

The “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” itself distinguishes them. One verse earlier it says, “The former friend Stokakrishna is Sri Purushottama Dasa” (130), and this “Dasa Purushottama” is not Sadashiva's son but another associate. Kanu Thakura's descendants, however, hold that he was Kanu's father, and the “First Vandana” says so as well. But the “Charitamrita” plainly names Sadashiva's son as Kanu's father, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, examining the question, follows the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”: Nagara Purushottama, the Vaidya, Sadashiva's son, is Dama, Krishna's friend in Vraja.3

The Name “Nagara”

Where the name “Nagara” comes from is explained in different ways. Some take it as a title (upadhi), others as the name of the region where he lived: the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” writes that he formerly lived in Nagara-desha. Hence his name Purushottama-Nagara.

By one explanation, fourteen villages (mauzas) — among them Beledanga, Berigram, Sukhasagara, Chandure, Manasapota and Palpara — belong to the pargana of Panchanagar, and so the region is sometimes called Nagaradesha.4

From Birth at Nityananda's Feet

Krishnadasa Kaviraja describes his nature:

“From his birth he was absorbed in the feet of Nityananda, and he ceaselessly played childhood games with Krishna.” (CC, Adi 11.39)

These games are neither a child's amusement nor a product of imagination. Purushottama is Krishna's eternal friend Dama, and from his very birth his eternal nature shone forth in him: friendship with Krishna, sakhya-rasa, and devotion to Nityananda, Balarama Himself, Whose companion he is. From his earliest years he constantly remembered Nityananda's feet. Krishnadasa Kaviraja counts him among the devotees, the branches, of Nityananda; in the headings of the edition of the “Charitamrita” with the “Anubhashya,” Sadashiva Kaviraja and Purushottama stand twenty-third and twenty-fourth.5

Vrindavana Dasa, naming him one of Nityananda's chief companions, says of him:

“Nityananda Chandra Himself played in the heart of Purushottama Dasa, and so there was not a trace of external awareness in his body.” (CB, Antya 5.742)

The Bengali verse has vihare — “plays”; the “First Vandana” repeats the same words: “Purushottama Dasa has no awareness of the external: Nityananda-chandra plays in his heart” (pt. 4, v. 35). This is neither illness nor worldly oblivion: he is wholly absorbed in prema and in the presence of Nityananda, Who unceasingly plays in his heart, and for him the external no longer exists.6

His disciple Devakinandana glorifies his guru in his “Vaishnava-vandana”:

“I praise my chosen master named Sri Purushottama — who can describe his incomparable qualities? Even one who has no good qualities he shows mercy to by the power of his natural compassion. In his seventh year he had the madness of love for Krishna; his dancing enchants the world, his power is unfathomable.” (Devakinandana, “Vaishnava-vandana,” 87–89)

Devakinandana goes on to tell of him also what the biographies do not record. Seizing Gauridasa the kirtaniya by the hair, Purushottama imparted his own power to him and made him sing the praise of Nityananda. Gadadhara Dasa and Sri Govinda Ghosha are named beside him — apparently as those before whom his greatness appeared and the Lord found joy. He was bathed in abhisheka with a hundred and eight pitchers of Ganga water; from childhood he was all-knowing. The karavi flower in his ear, before the whole assembly, came to smell like a lotus. Through his name all Vaishnavas attain perfection, and his body is the happiness of prema embodied (vv. 90–94). Jiva's Sanskrit vandana also tells of the karavi flower: “I praise the Dasa named Purushottama, endowed with majesty, who made the karavi flower in his ears smell like a lotus” (v. 94).7

Once, mad with prema, he swallowed snake venom — and suffered no harm at all. All who saw it marvelled at such unearthly (alaukika) power; so the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” relates. This is not magic, nor a wonder for its own sake: it is how the power of divine love, bestowed on him by Nityananda, shows itself. Many of Nityananda's companions displayed such power, and in this lies a trait shared by His whole circle.

The pada scholar Majumdar also counts Purushottama Dasa, Sadashiva's son, among the composers of padas. The “Padakalpataru” has several padas on Krishna's pastimes under this name (PK 1754–1758, 1762, 1868–1872, 1992), but he has many namesakes, and whose they are has not been settled; the biographies are silent about his padas.

Wife and Son

Jahnava was the name of Purushottama's wife; she is not Jahnava, the consort of Nityananda, but another Jahnava. A son was born to them, of whom Krishnadasa Kaviraja says:

“His son was the great soul Sri Kanu Thakura, whose body overflowed with the nectar of love for Krishna.” (CC, Adi 11.40)8

Soon after Kanu's birth his mother left this world — according to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” twelve days after his appearance. Hearing of it, Nityananda Prabhu went to Purushottama's home and carried the infant away with Him to Khardaha.9 According to the “Abhidhana,” He brought the child to His home and laid him on the lap of Mother Jahnava, His consort; one of the biographies says that Jahnava Devi adopted him. Seeing how devoted to Krishna the boy was from infancy, Nityananda named him Shishu Krishnadasa, “the child Krishnadasa.” Jiva's vandana glorifies him: “I praise the one called Shishu Krishnadasa, nurtured by Sri Nityananda, whose body is full of happiness, blessed and pure” (v. 133).

Shishu Krishnadasa was in his fifth year when Ishvari Jahnava Mata took him with her to Vrindavana. Seeing his bhava, Sri Jiva Gosvami and the other Vrajavasis named him Thakura Kanai. A tradition relates that once in Vrindavana, as he danced in kirtana, lost in bliss, the nupura — the ankle bell — slipped from his right foot and vanished. Kanai said, “Where this nupura has fallen, there I shall live.” The nupura, it is said, was found in the village of Bodhkhana in the district of Yashohar, in the courtyard of Sri Madana-mohana, as the “Abhidhana” adds; from then on Kanai lived there and founded his shripat, and by one of the biographies the nupura is kept to this day in the temple there, in Kanai's ancestral home. Bodhkhana is reached from Jhikargachha-ghat station on the Eastern Railway — by boat along the Kapotaksha River or overland, two to two and a half miles.

In Bodhkhana the ancient Deity of the family, Pranavallabha, is also served. According to family tradition, one of Sadashiva's ancestors served Him several centuries before the appearance of Sriman Mahaprabhu. Later, during the Bargi raids, the line of Kanai's eldest son stayed on in Bodhkhana, while the others, led by Vamshivadana, fled and settled in the village of Bhajanaghat in the district of Nadia. When the turmoil had subsided, Harikrishna Gosvami, from the youngest son's line, came back to Bodhkhana and installed a new Deity, also named Pranavallabha. Since then the eldest son's descendants serve the ancient Pranavallabha there, and the youngest son's the new one, while in Bhajanaghat Sri Radha-vallabha is served.

According to his descendants, Kanu Thakura appeared in the year 1457 of the Shaka era (942 of the Bengali era), on Thursday, shukla-dvitiya of the month of Ashadha, which was Ratha-yatra day.10 Some count him too among the twelve gopalas; the “Abhidhana” names him Ujjvala-gopala in the pastimes of Vraja. According to the “Prema-vilasa,” Kanu Thakura was at the festival in Kheturi together with Virabhadra Prabhu and Jahnava Devi: among the branches of Nityananda it names “Hariharananda, Kanu Thakura — a jewel of virtues” (19.146), and in the retinue of Jahnava, who came from Khardaha with Virachandra, “Kanai” (19.306–309). His disciples live in the village of Garbeta on the Shilavati River in the district of Medinipur; his famous disciple was the brahmana Shrirama, of the Rarhi brahmanas, of the “Sama-veda”'s Kauthumi branch.

Shripat and Deities

Purushottama's shripat was formerly in Sukhasagara, equidistant from the stations of Chakdaha and Simurali; according to the tradition of Kanu's descendants, cited by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, the village stood on the eastern bank of the Ganga.

The Deities installed by Purushottama formerly resided in Beledanga. When Beledanga was ruined, They were brought to Sukhasagara. When the river swallowed Sukhasagara too, They were brought, together with the Deities of the gadi — the seat — of Jahnava Mata, Nityananda's consort, which was in the same place, to Sahebdanga-Berigram; and when Berigram also was destroyed, to the village of Chandure.11 By the time Srila Bhaktisiddhanta wrote of this, the Deities had already resided in Chandure for some fifty years. Chandure lies on the Bhagirathi, in the district of Nadia, under the Chakdaha police station, a mile from Simurali station and a mile's walk from Palpara, upstream of it. Old Sukhasagara is no more — the river swallowed it; the new Sukhasagara lies south of Kaliganj, three or four miles from Chandure.

The temple in Chandure was then a simple hut with a thatched roof and mud walls. In it were served Sri Jagannatha, Balarama and Subhadra, two pairs of Nitai-Gaura, Gopinatha, Jahnava Mata, Bala-gopala, five pairs of Radha-Govinda, Revati and Balarama, and a shalagrama. Purushottama Thakura himself installed some of these shri-murtis; the rest, it is said, came from Jahnava Devi's gadi. The shripat is also known as “the pat of Vasu and Jahnava,” after the names of Nityananda's consorts. Service here passed from mahanta to mahanta: Gopala Dasa Mahanta, Ramakrishna, Vihari Dasa, Rama Dasa, another Gopala Dasa and, at that time, the aged Sitanatha Dasa. The Deities of Purushottama, brought to Chandure (Chanduria) after the loss of Sukhasagara, were at that time, according to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, served together with his other Deities under the supervision of the line of Ganga of Jirat.

Disciples

His disciple was Devakinandana Dasa, the author of the “Vaishnava-vandana”; the vandana itself says so, and therefore Devakinandana belonged to the family of Nityananda. Manohara Dasa writes:

“Sri Purushottama Mahashaya, dear to Nityananda — his disciple is Sri Devakinandana Thakura. In the ‘Vaishnava-vandana’ that he composed he wrote of the four sampradayas.” (“Anuraga-valli” 8.44–45)

Devakinandana himself calls him his guru: in the Bengali vandana, “my chosen master” (v. 87), and in the Sanskrit “Vaishnavabhidhana” he begins by bowing “to my guru Sri Purushottama, whose merciful glance has purified the earth — a wish-fulfilling tree that grants every desire” (pt. 3, v. 1), and, listing Nityananda's companions, he calls him “my supreme one — Srila Sri Purushottama” (v. 31). Devakinandana was his mantra disciple.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta quotes lines about his four dearest disciples, the best of brahmanas: first Madhavacharya, then Yadavacharya Pandita and Daivakinandana (Devakinandana) Dasa; the fourth is not named. One of the biographies names three chief disciples — Madhavacharya, Yadavacharya and Devakinandana, all three from brahmana families.12 About Madhavacharya — Madhava Chattopadhyaya of Jirat, the husband of Ganga, Nityananda's daughter — opinions differ: some hold him a disciple of Nityananda Prabhu Himself, others of Jahnava Devi, still others of Purushottama Thakura. Both Purushottama and Kanu Thakura counted many brahmanas by birth (shaukra brahmanas) among their disciples.

Departure

Where and when Purushottama Dasa appeared in this world and when he withdrew from it, the sources do not say; nor do they tell how he first met Mahaprabhu and Nityananda. According to our calendar, the appearance day of Srila Purushottama Thakura is gaura-chaturthi of the month of Govinda, and his disappearance day is krishna-panchami of the same month — the same day as the appearance of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati.13 The year and place of his departure have not come down to us.

Significance

Purushottama Dasa is Krishna's eternal friend Dama, who came into Gaura's pastimes as a companion of Nityananda. From birth he was absorbed in service to Nityananda's feet and always played with Krishna, and Nityananda Himself played in his heart, so that for him nothing external existed.

His family shows how generous the Lord's mercy is: four generations in a row, from grandfather to son, were perfected associates of Gaura. The power of his prema, revealed in the madness of love, is the same that lived in all of Nityananda's circle. And through his disciple Devakinandana his name entered the “Vaishnava-vandana,” where all the Lord's associates are glorified.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his many namesakes: Purushottama Pandita of Navadvipa (CC, Adi 11.33), Purushottama Brahmachari (CC, Adi 12.62), the sannyasi Purushottama Tirtha (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 101), Purushottama, son of Ratnakara, of Nadia (Devakinandana, “Vaishnava-vandana,” 97), Purushottama Datta, Purushottama Sanjaya, Purushottama Jana and King Purushottama-deva, nor with the Purushottama in the retinue of Advaita's sons (“Prema-vilasa” 19.318), nor with Purushottama-kshetra, Puri. His wife Jahnava is not Jahnava, Nityananda's consort; his son Kanu Thakura is not Kanai Thakura of Shrikhanda, the son of Raghunandana.
  2. One of the biographies calls this cowherd boy “Daman”; in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (131) he is Dama, and so too in the “Anubhashya.”
  3. According to the tradition of Kanu Thakura's descendants (reported by one of the biographies and by the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana”), Kanu's father was not “Nagara Purushottama” but the “Dasa Purushottama” of the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (130), Stokakrishna in Vraja. So too the “First Vandana”: “The one whom the Puranas extol as Stokakrishna — all know: it is Purushottama” (pt. 4, v. 36). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” (to CC, Adi 11.40) answers this: in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” it is precisely Sadashiva's son, the Vaidya, who is called Nagara Purushottama — in Vraja the friend Dama; and the “Charitamrita” (Adi 11.38–40) plainly makes Sadashiva's son the father of Kanu, while the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” calls this son Purushottama Dasa. The biography gives the descendants' view without this answer. We follow the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (131) and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta.
  4. One of the biographies gives this explanation in brackets within a quotation from the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” but it is not in that work's article on Purushottama-Nagara. It goes back to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's “Anubhashya” on the verse about Mahesha Pandita (CC, Adi 11.32): Palpara belongs to the pargana of Panchanagar, which has fourteen mauzas, and so some call these parts Nagardesh; Purushottama is not mentioned there. Another biography speaks only of five villages — Beledanga, Berigram, Sukhasagara, Manasapota and Palpara — which lie so close together that the region is sometimes called Nagaradesha; it does not name Chandure.
  5. This numbering belongs to the headings of the edition (as does “Purushottama, the tenth gopala”), not to the words of the “Charitamrita” itself; one of the biographies presents it as Krishnadasa Kaviraja's own words.
  6. One of the biographies puts it thus: “Nityananda is constantly acting through him.” The “Anubhashya” gives this passage of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” as “Antya, ch. 6,” following the old division of chapters; in our edition it is Antya 5.741–742.
  7. In another vandana, the tripadi of the “second” Vrindavana Dasa (pt. 5, v. 68), the same wonder of the karavi flower is ascribed to Gadadhara Dasa (with whom Vasudeva Ghosha is glorified there).
  8. One of the biographies renders this verse of the “Charitamrita” (Adi 11.40) as if Krishna always lived in Kanu Thakura's body; the Bengali says that his body was full of the nectar of love for Krishna.
  9. One of the biographies, following the “Anubhashya,” says that Nityananda took “a twelve-year-old child,” yet at once reports that in his fifth year the boy went with Jahnava to Vrindavana. The “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” speaks of “a twelve-day-old infant,” other biographies say that the mother left right after his birth or “when the son was still very small.” Most likely twelve days are meant; we write “the infant.”
  10. According to another biography, Kanu Thakura appeared on Ratha-yatra day in 1450 Shaka; in the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” the year seems to be 1453. We do not reconcile these dates.
  11. One of the biographies understands this as though the Deities were moved from Berigram to Chandure “some three or four miles”; in Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, three or four miles is the distance from Chandure to the new Sukhasagara.
  12. In this biography Madhavacharya is called “Madhvacharya” — not the founder of the sampradaya, but Madhavacharya of Jirat, Ganga's husband. Yadavacharya Pandita is not Yadavacharya Gosani of Vrindavana: they have not been shown to be the same.
  13. Which Purushottama is honoured on these days the calendar does not specify; in Gaudiya Vaishnava calendars they are usually associated with Purushottama Dasa of the twelve gopalas.
